questions.question: What is try-with-resources in Java and why was it introduced?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources in Java Explained
questions.direct_answer: **try-with-resources** (Java 7) declares resources in the `try(...)` header and **auto-closes** them when the block exits — normally or via exception. It replaces the error-prone manual `try`/`finally` close pattern, where a forgotten or throwing `close()` caused resource leaks. Any resource that implements **`AutoCloseable`** is eligible, and they close in **reverse order** of declaration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know try-with-resources auto-closes AutoCloseable resources and why it replaced manual finally-close
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Still writing manual finally blocks to close resources, or not null-checking before close in the old pattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it also fixes the suppressed-exception problem: a failure in close() no longer hides the original try exception

sections.title: What try-with-resources Is
sections.content:
**try-with-resources** is a Java 7 feature that closes a resource for you automatically. A **resource** is anything you must release after use — a file, a stream, a database `Connection`. You declare it inside the `try(...)` header, and when the block exits, the JVM calls its `close()` method for you.

It exists because the old way was easy to get wrong. Before Java 7, you closed a resource yourself in a `finally` block. That meant remembering a `null` check, remembering to call `close()`, and hoping `close()` didn't throw and hide the real error.

**How it works:** any resource that implements **`AutoCloseable`** is eligible — streams, readers, `Connection`, `Statement`, `ResultSet`. When the block ends, Java closes it, whether the code finished normally or threw.

- **Auto-close** — no `finally` needed
- **Reverse order** — multiple resources close last-opened-first
- **Suppressed exceptions** — a failing `close()` never hides the original error

> **Key rule:** the resource must implement `AutoCloseable`, and it is effectively final inside the header — you can't reassign it.

sections.content:
emerald|Declare in header|~try (Resource r = ...)|since Java 7|r must be AutoCloseable|scoped to the block
blue|Auto-close|~close() called for you|on normal exit|and on exception|no finally needed
amber|Reverse order|~Last opened, first closed|like a stack|matches dependencies|safe teardown
rose|Suppressed exceptions|~close() failure recorded|original still propagates|getSuppressed() to see them|no lost errors

sections.title: How try-with-resources Runs
sections.content:
Follow the path the JVM takes when the block exits — close always happens, on both branches.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Open resource in try(...) header"] --> B["Run the try body"]
    B --> C{"Exception thrown?"}
    C -->|No| D["JVM calls close()"]
    C -->|Yes| E["JVM calls close() first"]
    E --> F{"close() also throws?"}
    F -->|No| G["Original exception propagates"]
    F -->|Yes| H["close failure attached as suppressed"]
    D --> I["Block exits cleanly"]
```

The key insight: the `close()` call sits on **every** exit path, so a resource can never leak.

sections.title: Without try-with-resources: fragile manual close
With try-with-resources: auto-closed and leak-free
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Still writing manual `finally` close** when try-with-resources would be simpler and safer.
- **Forgetting the resource must implement `AutoCloseable`** — otherwise it won't compile in the header.
- **Assuming close order is declaration order** — it's *reverse*.
- **Reassigning the resource variable** — try-with-resources resources are effectively final.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Java 7 feature** that auto-closes resources declared in the `try(...)` header.
- **Replaces manual `try`/`finally`** close, eliminating leaks and null-check boilerplate.
- **Works with any `AutoCloseable`** resource; closes in **reverse** order.
- **Records `close()` failures as suppressed exceptions**, preserving the original.
- **Resource variables are effectively final** — you can't reassign them.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Try-with-resources is a feature added in Java 7 that automatically closes resources for you. The way it works is you declare the resource inside parentheses right after the try keyword, and then when the block exits — whether it finishes normally or because an exception was thrown — the JVM automatically calls close on that resource. The reason it was introduced is that the old way of doing this was genuinely error-prone. Before Java 7, you'd declare the resource, use it in the try block, and then close it in a finally block. But that pattern had several pitfalls. You had to remember a null check before closing, you might forget to close it at all and leak the resource, and worst of all, if the close call itself threw an exception, it would replace and hide the original exception from the try block. Try-with-resources solves all of those. Any resource that implements the AutoCloseable interface is eligible — that's things like input and output streams, readers, and J D B C objects like Connection, Statement, and ResultSet. If you declare multiple resources, they're closed in reverse order of how you declared them, like unwinding a stack, which is exactly what you want when later resources depend on earlier ones. And there's a really nice bonus around exceptions: if both your try block and the close call throw, the close failure gets attached to the original exception as a suppressed exception, instead of overwriting it. So you keep the real cause and can still see what went wrong during cleanup by calling getSuppressed. Overall it's less code, safer, and it's the idiomatic way to handle resources in modern Java.

questions.question: What is AutoCloseable and how does it relate to try-with-resources?
questions.title: AutoCloseable Interface and Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: **`AutoCloseable`** is the single-method interface (`void close() throws Exception`) that makes a class usable in try-with-resources. When you declare such an object in the `try(...)` header, the JVM calls its `close()` automatically. **`Closeable`** (from `java.io`) extends `AutoCloseable` but narrows `close()` to throw only `IOException`. Implement `AutoCloseable` on your own classes to get automatic cleanup.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know AutoCloseable is the contract behind try-with-resources and can implement it on a custom class
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Closeable and AutoCloseable, or thinking only JDK classes can be used in try-with-resources
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note Closeable extends AutoCloseable and predates it (Java 5 vs 7), and that close() should be idempotent

sections.title: The Contract Behind try-with-resources
sections.content:
**`AutoCloseable`** is an interface with exactly one method: `void close() throws Exception`. Any class that implements it can be used in try-with-resources — that's the whole contract. When you put such an object in the `try(...)` header, the compiler guarantees `close()` runs when the block exits.

It exists so try-with-resources has a single, standard target. The feature needs to know one thing about a resource: that it can close itself. **`AutoCloseable`** is that promise.

**`Closeable`** (in `java.io`, since Java 5) is the older, narrower interface. It **extends `AutoCloseable`** and restricts `close()` to throw only `IOException`. So every `Closeable` is an `AutoCloseable`, but not the other way around.

- **`AutoCloseable`** — root contract, `close()` throws `Exception`
- **`Closeable`** — I/O subinterface, `close()` throws `IOException`
- **Your class** — just `implements AutoCloseable` and releases what it holds

> **Key rule:** make `close()` idempotent — calling it twice should be safe, since manual and automatic calls can overlap.

sections.title: AutoCloseable vs Closeable
sections.content:
emerald|AutoCloseable|~Java 7, root contract|close() throws Exception|enables try-with-resources|any resource type
blue|Closeable|~Java 5, java.io|extends AutoCloseable|close() throws IOException only|streams, readers
amber|Your class|~implements AutoCloseable|release in close()|works in try header|make close() idempotent
rose|Common trap|~They're not unrelated|Closeable IS-A AutoCloseable|not the other way|narrower exception

sections.title: How the Interfaces Relate
sections.content:
Read the arrows as is-a: `Closeable` is an `AutoCloseable`, never the reverse. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["AutoCloseable
close() throws Exception"] --> B["Closeable
close() throws IOException"] A --> C["Your custom class
implements AutoCloseable"] B --> D["BufferedReader, InputStream"] A --> E["JDBC: Connection, Statement, ResultSet"] ``` Everything under `AutoCloseable` works in a try-with-resources header — JDK types and your own classes alike.

sections.title: A Custom AutoCloseable Resource
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing `Closeable` and `AutoCloseable`.** `Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable` and is narrower (only `IOException`).
- **Thinking only JDK classes qualify.** Any class that `implements AutoCloseable` works in try-with-resources.
- **A `close()` that isn't idempotent.** Calling it twice (manual + auto) should be safe.
- **Throwing broadly from `close()`.** Prefer narrowing the declared exception if your cleanup can't fail.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`AutoCloseable.close()`** is the method try-with-resources calls automatically.
- **`Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable`** (Java 5 vs 7) and narrows `close()` to `IOException`.
- **Implement `AutoCloseable`** on your own classes for automatic cleanup.
- **`close()` should be idempotent** — safe to call more than once.
- **You can narrow the exception** `close()` declares (e.g., throw nothing).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: AutoCloseable is the interface that makes try-with-resources work. It's essentially a functional interface with a single method, close, which is declared to throw Exception. Any object whose class implements AutoCloseable can be declared in the try-with-resources header, and the compiler then guarantees that its close method gets called when the block exits, whether normally or because of an exception. So AutoCloseable is the contract, and try-with-resources is the language feature that consumes it. There's a closely related interface called Closeable, which lives in the java dot i o package and actually predates AutoCloseable — Closeable came in Java 5, AutoCloseable in Java 7. The relationship people often get backwards is that Closeable extends AutoCloseable, not the other way around. Closeable is the narrower one: it restricts close to throw only an I O exception rather than the broader Exception. So every Closeable is automatically an AutoCloseable, which is why all the classic java dot i o streams work in try-with-resources, but the reverse isn't true. The other thing worth saying is that this isn't limited to JDK classes. You can make your own class auto-closeable just by implementing AutoCloseable and putting your cleanup logic — releasing a connection, a lock, a native handle — inside the close method. A good practice is to make close idempotent, meaning calling it twice does no harm, because in some situations it could be invoked both manually and automatically. And if your cleanup can't actually throw a checked exception, you're allowed to narrow the signature and declare that close throws nothing, which is cleaner for callers.

questions.question: Can try-with-resources be used without a catch block?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources Without Catch Block
questions.direct_answer: Yes. try-with-resources can stand alone with **no `catch` and no `finally`** — `try (Resource r = ...) { ... }` is valid. The resource is still auto-closed, and any exception simply **propagates to the caller**. You add a `catch` only if you actually want to handle the exception here; otherwise the bare form is perfectly fine.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know try-with-resources is itself a complete statement that doesn't require catch or finally
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you must add a catch (or finally) when using try-with-resources
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify that the implicit close acts like a finally, so adding an explicit finally is usually redundant

sections.title: try-with-resources Is Complete on Its Own
sections.content:
**Yes — a try-with-resources can stand alone**, with no `catch` and no `finally`. So `try (Resource r = open()) { use(r); }` compiles and runs fine on its own.

Why it works: normally a `try` needs a `catch` or a `finally`. But **try-with-resources counts as that required clause** — the resource declaration carries an implicit close that behaves like a `finally`.

**What happens on the way out:** the resource is closed automatically, and if anything throws, the exception **propagates to the caller** unhandled. Closing and exception handling are two separate jobs.

- **Bare form** — `try(r) { ... }`, exception propagates
- **With `catch`** — handle the error here when you can recover
- **With `finally`** — only for extra cleanup beyond closing

> **Key rule:** if the propagating exception is checked (like `IOException`), your method must declare `throws` — the implicit close doesn't change that.

sections.title: Forms of try-with-resources
sections.content:
emerald|Bare form|~No catch, no finally|try (r = ...) { ... }|valid & common|exception propagates
blue|With catch|~Handle here|try (r=...) {..} catch {..}|when you can recover|close still happens first
amber|With finally|~Usually redundant|close is automatic|finally for extra cleanup only|rarely needed
rose|Implicit close|~Acts like finally|satisfies the try rule|runs before catch|reverse order if multiple

sections.title: Catch Is Optional, Close Is Not
sections.content:
The decision is only about who handles the error — the close runs either way.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["try (resource) { ... }"] --> B["Block exits, JVM closes the resource"]
    B --> C{"Did the body throw?"}
    C -->|No| D["Method returns normally"]
    C -->|Yes| E{"Is there a catch here?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Handle it locally"]
    E -->|No| G["Exception propagates to caller"]
```

Notice the close in step two happens before the catch decision — handling is a separate concern.

sections.title: Standalone try-with-resources (no catch)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking a `catch` is mandatory.** The implicit close satisfies the `try` requirement.
- **Adding a redundant `finally` to close** — try-with-resources already closes for you.
- **Forgetting to declare/propagate the checked exception** when there's no `catch` (`throws IOException`).
- **Swallowing with an empty `catch`** just to avoid declaring `throws` — let it propagate instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Bare try-with-resources is valid** — no `catch`, no `finally` required.
- **The implicit close acts as the `finally`**, satisfying the language rule.
- **Unhandled exceptions propagate** to the caller (declare `throws` if checked).
- **Add `catch` only to handle** the exception locally.
- **An explicit `finally` is usually redundant** for closing resources.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, you can use try-with-resources completely on its own, with no catch block and no finally block. Normally the rule is that a plain try has to be followed by a catch or a finally, but with try-with-resources, the resource declaration itself satisfies that requirement, because it carries an implicit close that behaves just like a finally. So writing try, open your resource in the parentheses, use it in the body, and then nothing after the closing brace — that compiles and runs perfectly. When the block exits, the resource's close method is called automatically, and if an exception was thrown, it just propagates up to the caller unhandled. The one thing you need to remember is that if the exception is checked, like an I O exception, and you're not catching it, then your method has to declare it with throws, because you're passing the responsibility up the chain. You only add a catch block when you genuinely want to handle the error at this level — for instance, to log it and return a default value. And adding an explicit finally is allowed, but for the purpose of closing the resource it's redundant, because that's exactly what try-with-resources is already doing for you. The only reason you'd add a finally is if you have some additional cleanup beyond closing the declared resources. A mistake I'd avoid is adding an empty catch block just to dodge declaring throws, because that swallows the exception and hides problems. If you can't handle it meaningfully, it's better to let it propagate.

questions.question: Can you declare multiple resources in a try-with-resources statement?
questions.title: Multiple Resources in Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: Yes. Declare multiple resources in one `try(...)` header, separated by **semicolons**: `try (var a = ...; var b = ...) { }`. They are **closed in reverse order** of declaration (last opened, first closed), which safely unwinds dependencies. Each resource gets its own `close()` call even if an earlier one throws while closing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know multiple resources are semicolon-separated and closed in reverse declaration order
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using commas instead of semicolons, or assuming close order matches declaration order
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why reverse order matters when one resource depends on another (e.g., ResultSet before Statement before Connection)

sections.title: Several Resources, Closed in Reverse
sections.content:
**Yes — declare any number of resources in one header**, separated by **semicolons**: `try (A a = ...; B b = ...) { ... }`. This is cleaner than nesting a separate `try` for each one.

**Opening order is left to right**, just as you wrote them. When the block exits, the resources are **closed in the reverse order** — the last one opened is the first one closed, exactly like unwinding a stack.

Why reverse? Because resources often depend on each other. A `ResultSet` is built from a `Statement`, which is built from a `Connection`, so you want them closed `ResultSet` → `Statement` → `Connection`.

- **Semicolon-separated** — not commas
- **Opened** left to right
- **Closed** right to left (reverse)

> **Key rule:** even if one `close()` throws, the remaining resources still close — the failure is recorded as suppressed, so nothing leaks.

sections.title: Multiple Resources Rules
sections.content:
emerald|Semicolon-separated|~Not commas|try (A a=..; B b=..)|any count allowed|each is closed
amber|Reverse close order|~Last opened, first closed|like a stack|safe for dependencies|automatic
blue|JDBC example|~ResultSet -> Statement -> Connection|child before parent|avoids 'closed' errors|natural unwind
rose|All still close|~Even if one throws|remaining closes run|failures suppressed|no leaks

sections.title: Open Left-to-Right, Close Right-to-Left
sections.content:
Resources unwind like a stack — the order is automatic and dependency-safe.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Open A"] --> B["Open B"]
    B --> C["Open C"]
    C --> D["Run the try body"]
    D --> E["close() on C"]
    E --> F["close() on B"]
    F --> G["close() on A"]
```

The last resource opened (C) is the first one closed — child before parent.

sections.title: Declaring and Closing Multiple Resources
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using commas instead of semicolons** between resources — won't compile.
- **Assuming declaration order = close order.** It's the *reverse*.
- **Manually closing in the wrong order** in legacy code — leads to 'connection already closed' errors.
- **Cramming unrelated resources** into one header when separate try blocks would read clearer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multiple resources are semicolon-separated** in the `try(...)` header.
- **Closed in reverse declaration order** (last opened, first closed).
- **Reverse order respects dependencies** — e.g., `ResultSet` before `Connection`.
- **All resources close** even if one `close()` throws.
- **Cleaner than nested try blocks** for related resources.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, you can declare multiple resources in a single try-with-resources statement, and you separate them with semicolons inside the parentheses — not commas, which is a common slip. So you might write try, open resource A, semicolon, open resource B, close the parentheses, and then use both in the body. This is much cleaner than the old approach of nesting a separate try block for every resource. The detail interviewers like to check is the close order. The resources are closed in the reverse order of how you declared them — the last one you opened is the first one closed, just like unwinding a stack. And that reverse ordering isn't arbitrary; it's exactly what you want when the resources depend on each other. The classic example is J D B C, where you open a Connection, then create a Statement from that connection, then get a ResultSet from the statement. You want to close them in the opposite direction — ResultSet first, then Statement, then Connection — because closing the parent before the child can cause already-closed errors. Try-with-resources gives you that correct order for free. Another nice guarantee is that every resource gets its close called, even if one of the earlier closes throws an exception. The remaining closes still run, so you never leak a resource just because cleanup of a sibling failed, and any close failures are recorded as suppressed exceptions. The one bit of judgement I'd apply is not to cram a bunch of unrelated resources into a single header just because you can — if they're logically separate, separate try blocks can read more clearly.

questions.question: How does try-with-resources work with JDBC — Connection, Statement, and ResultSet?
questions.title: Try-With-Resources with JDBC
questions.direct_answer: In JDBC, `Connection`, `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`, and `ResultSet` all implement `AutoCloseable`, so declare them in a try-with-resources header and they auto-close in **reverse order** (`ResultSet` → `Statement` → `Connection`). This eliminates the classic leak where a forgotten `close()` exhausts the connection pool. Prefer `PreparedStatement` for parameters to avoid SQL injection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply try-with-resources to the real JDBC trio and know why leaking connections is catastrophic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Closing only the Connection (not Statement/ResultSet), or building queries with string concatenation instead of PreparedStatement
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that leaked connections exhaust the pool and take the whole service down, and that PreparedStatement also prevents SQL injection

sections.title: JDBC Is the Textbook Case for try-with-resources
sections.content:
**In JDBC, the three core types close themselves** when you use try-with-resources. `Connection`, `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`, and `ResultSet` all implement `AutoCloseable`, so declaring them in the header closes each one automatically in **reverse order**: `ResultSet` first, then the statement, then the `Connection`.

Why this matters so much is the **connection pool**. A `Connection` isn't a cheap throwaway object — it's a slot in a **fixed-size pool**. Leak enough of them and the pool runs dry.

**What a leak does:** once the pool is exhausted, every new request blocks waiting for a connection that never comes back, and the whole service grinds to a halt. try-with-resources makes that leak almost impossible.

- **Close all three** — `ResultSet`, statement, `Connection`
- **Reverse order** — child before parent
- **Use `PreparedStatement`** with bind parameters

> **Key rule:** bind parameters with `?` instead of concatenating user input — this prevents SQL injection and lets the driver reuse the statement.

sections.title: The JDBC Trio
sections.content:
blue|Connection|~Pool slot, scarce|implements AutoCloseable|leaking exhausts the pool|closed LAST
emerald|PreparedStatement|~Parameterized query|implements AutoCloseable|prevents SQL injection|closed second
amber|ResultSet|~Query rows cursor|implements AutoCloseable|tied to its statement|closed FIRST
rose|The leak|~Forgotten close()|pool runs dry|requests block / time out|service outage

sections.title: Why a Leaked Connection Kills the Service
sections.content:
Each un-closed `ResultSet` pins its statement, which pins its connection — and the pool drains.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request opens a Connection"] --> B["Query runs, ResultSet not closed"]
    B --> C["ResultSet pins Statement pins Connection"]
    C --> D["Pool slot never returned"]
    D --> E{"Pool exhausted?"}
    E -->|No| A
    E -->|Yes| F["New requests block, service stalls"]
```

try-with-resources breaks this loop: all three close in the right order on every path.

sections.title: Wrong: string-built query + manual close that leaks
Right: try-with-resources + PreparedStatement
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Closing only the `Connection`.** The `Statement` and `ResultSet` leak too — declare all three.
- **String-concatenating SQL.** Use `PreparedStatement` with `?` parameters to stop SQL injection.
- **Leaking on the error path.** Manual code that closes only on success still leaks when a query throws.
- **Holding the connection too long.** Open late, close early; don't span unrelated work.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Connection`, `Statement`, `ResultSet` are all `AutoCloseable`** — use try-with-resources.
- **Closed in reverse**: `ResultSet` → `Statement` → `Connection`.
- **Leaked connections exhaust the pool** and can take down the whole service.
- **`PreparedStatement` with `?`** prevents SQL injection and is reusable.
- **Open late, close early** to free pool slots quickly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: J D B C is the textbook example for try-with-resources, because all three of the core types — Connection, Statement or PreparedStatement, and ResultSet — implement AutoCloseable. So you declare them in the try header, and they get closed automatically in reverse order: the ResultSet closes first, then the statement, then the Connection. That reverse order is correct because the ResultSet depends on the statement and the statement depends on the connection. Why this matters so much is the connection pool. A Connection isn't a cheap throwaway object — it's a slot in a fixed-size pool. If you leak connections by forgetting to close them, especially on the error path, the pool slowly drains. Once it's exhausted, every new request just blocks waiting for a connection that never comes back, and the whole service effectively goes down. I've seen that be the root cause of real outages. With try-with-resources, that leak becomes almost impossible, because the close happens whether the query succeeds or throws. The other best practice I'd pair with this is using PreparedStatement with bind parameters — the question marks — rather than concatenating user input into the S Q L string. That does two things: it prevents S Q L injection, and the statement can be reused and cached by the driver. So the strong answer combines both: try-with-resources for guaranteed cleanup of the connection, statement, and result set, and PreparedStatement for safe, parameterized queries. And a small operational tip — open the connection as late as you can and let it close as early as possible, so you're not holding a scarce pool slot during unrelated work.

questions.question: What are suppressed exceptions in try-with-resources?
questions.title: Suppressed Exceptions in Try-With-Resources
questions.direct_answer: A **suppressed exception** happens when the `try` body throws *and* the resource's `close()` also throws. try-with-resources keeps the **original (try) exception** as primary and attaches the `close()` failure as a **suppressed** exception (retrievable via `getSuppressed()`). The old manual `finally` pattern did the opposite — the close exception replaced and hid the real one.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand which exception is primary when both the body and close() throw, and how to retrieve the other
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the close() exception wins (as in manual finally) and that the original is lost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with manual try-finally where the close exception masked the real one, and mention addSuppressed/getSuppressed

sections.title: When Both the Body and close() Fail
sections.content:
A **suppressed exception** is the secondary error that try-with-resources records when *two* things fail at once: your `try` body throws, and then the resource's `close()` throws too. You now have two exceptions but can only propagate one.

**How try-with-resources resolves it:** the **exception from the `try` body is primary** and propagates to the caller. The `close()` failure is attached to it as a **suppressed** exception — recorded, not lost.

**Reading them back:** you call **`getSuppressed()`** on the primary exception (the JVM attaches them via `addSuppressed()`). In a stack trace they appear under a `Suppressed:` label.

- **Primary** — from the `try` body, propagates
- **Suppressed** — from `close()`, attached
- **`getSuppressed()`** — reads the attached ones

> **Key rule:** this is the opposite of the old manual `finally`, where a throwing `close()` *replaced* the original and hid the real cause.

sections.title: Suppressed Exceptions Explained
sections.content:
emerald|Primary exception|~From the try body|the real cause|propagates to caller|kept intact
amber|Suppressed exception|~From close()|attached, not lost|getSuppressed() to read|shown as 'Suppressed:' in trace
rose|Old finally pattern|~close() exception won|original replaced|real cause hidden|why try-with-resources is better
blue|API|~addSuppressed / getSuppressed|on Throwable|JVM wires it up|you rarely call them directly

sections.title: Which Exception Reaches the Caller
sections.content:
Both errors survive — one as primary, one attached underneath it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["try body throws (primary)"] --> B["JVM calls close()"]
    B --> C{"close() throws too?"}
    C -->|No| D["Primary propagates alone"]
    C -->|Yes| E["close failure added via addSuppressed()"]
    E --> F["Primary propagates to caller"]
    F --> G["getSuppressed() reveals the close failure"]
```

The body error always wins the race to the caller; the close failure rides along.

sections.title: Primary vs Suppressed in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming the `close()` exception wins.** In try-with-resources, the *body* exception is primary.
- **Forgetting `getSuppressed()` exists.** The close failure is still recorded — go read it.
- **Replicating the old `finally` bug** by manually closing and rethrowing in a way that drops the original.
- **Ignoring 'Suppressed:' lines** in a stack trace — they often explain a secondary cleanup failure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Suppressed = `close()` threw while the body was already throwing.**
- **The body exception is primary**; the close failure is attached, not lost.
- **Retrieve via `getSuppressed()`** (JVM adds via `addSuppressed()`).
- **Opposite of manual `finally`**, where the close exception used to mask the real one.
- **Stack traces show suppressed exceptions** under a 'Suppressed:' label.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Suppressed exceptions come up in a very specific situation: your try block throws an exception, and then while try-with-resources is cleaning up, the resource's close method also throws. Now you've got two exceptions, but only one can actually propagate out of the method. Try-with-resources handles this in a really sensible way — it treats the exception from the try body as the primary one, the one that propagates to the caller, and it attaches the close failure to it as a suppressed exception. So nothing is lost: the real cause stays primary, and the cleanup failure is recorded on the side. You can get to those suppressed exceptions by calling getSuppressed on the primary exception, which returns an array, and under the hood the JVM attaches them using addSuppressed. In a stack trace, you'll see them printed under a Suppressed label. The reason this is such a nice improvement is that it's the opposite of what the old manual try-finally pattern did. In the old pattern, if your finally block called close and close threw, that close exception would replace the original exception from the try block. So you'd lose the real cause — the thing that actually broke — and only see the secondary cleanup failure, which made debugging really painful. The common misconception is that the close exception wins, because that's how the old pattern worked, but with try-with-resources it's the body exception that wins and the close exception that gets suppressed. So if I'm debugging and I see a Suppressed line in a trace, I know that's a secondary failure that happened during cleanup, and the main exception above it is the one to focus on first.
